title: The basket in the reeds (Exodus 2:1–10)
hook: a mother, a sister watching, and Pharaoh's daughter who pities the child

segments.voice: Yesterday, the midwives: Shiphrah and Puah feared God more than Pharaoh and let the boys live. Your line was two women said no.

Pharaoh's order is out: every Hebrew baby boy goes into the Nile. In one house of the tribe of Levi, a boy is born. His mother sees, the text says, that he's a goodly child. So she hides him. One month. Two. Three. Three months of a newborn: the crying at three in the morning, the neighbors, the thin walls. When she can't hide him any longer, she does something that sounds like obeying the order and is the opposite. She puts her son in the Nile. Just not the way Pharaoh meant.
screen: `EVERY BOY INTO THE NILE.` → `THREE MONTHS OF HIDING.` → `INTO THE NILE, HER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the basket. She takes a basket of papyrus reeds, seals it with tar and pitch, lays the baby inside, and sets it among the reeds at the river's edge. The Hebrew word for this basket is tevah, the same word Genesis uses for Noah's ark: a boat that carries life through deadly water, this time the size of a baby. Second, the sister. She stands at a distance, the text says, to see what will happen. She isn't named here; later the Bible names Moses's sister as Miriam, and tradition takes her to be this girl. Third, Pharaoh's daughter. She comes down to bathe, sees the basket, sends her maid to fetch it, and opens it. The baby is crying. She has compassion on him, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is one of the babes of the Hebrews." She knows exactly what he is, and whose order he's under: her father's. And she pities him anyway. Fourth, the sister's move. Quick as anything, she steps out: shall I go and find you a nurse from the Hebrew women? Go, says the princess, and the girl fetches the baby's own mother. Pharaoh's daughter even pays her to nurse her own son. When he's older, the princess adopts him and names him Moses, because, she says, she drew him out of the water. So count the women before Moses says a single word: two midwives, a mother, a sister, a princess. The king's plan was to drown the boys. Every one of those women undid it.
screen: `A TEVAH: THE SAME WORD AS NOAH'S ARK.` · `A SISTER STANDS AT A DISTANCE.` · `ONE OF THE BABES OF THE HEBREWS.` · `DRAWN OUT OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who can't fully protect themselves: a child, a new neighbor still learning the language, an elderly relative, a kid at school who sits alone. The sister in the reeds didn't rescue anyone; she stayed close enough to see, and spoke up at the right moment, so picture where you could stand and keep watch. If you pray, hold them before God by name; if you don't, simply keep them in view.
Tevah, the Hebrew word for basket, the same one used for Noah's ark: a boat that carried baby Moses through deadly water. Today's word.
Your line: a sister watched. Drawn out of the water, by many hands. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Matthew's Gospel tells of the infant Jesus carried to safety in Egypt when Herod ordered the boys of Bethlehem killed, and Catholic preaching sometimes sets that rescue beside the infant Moses saved from a king's order.

chat.says: Why does the Bible use the same word for Moses's basket and Noah's ark?
options: Both are a tevah: a boat that carries life through deadly water.
Because Hebrew had just one word for anything that floated on water.
Because the basket was built big, like a ship for the whole family.
chat.meaning: Genesis calls Noah's ark a tevah, and Exodus uses the same word for the basket: each time, a small vessel carries life through water meant for death.

notes: Tevah used only for Noah's ark (Genesis 6–9) and Moses's basket (Exodus 2:3, 5): standard observation; confirm.
The sister is unnamed in Exodus 2; identified with Miriam by tradition (Numbers 26:59 names Miriam as sister of Moses and Aaron). Confirm.
Exodus 2:6 ('this is one of the Hebrews' children') is KJV wording, used unquoted in the voice; treat as paraphrase or confirm DR wording.
Name Moses: Hebrew wordplay with mashah (to draw out) and the Egyptian element ms/mose (born of, son, as in Thutmose); confirm the trapdoor wording.
